summary: A C string is not a type but a convention: a sequence of char values ending with a zero byte, '\0', stored in an array and passed around by the address of its first character. Every string function, from printf to strlen, walks memory until it finds that terminator. This makes strings cheap and flexible and also the most common place for buffer overflows, missing terminators and writes to read-only literals. Text handling in parsers, protocols, file paths, command lines and kernels all rests on these rules.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
C has no string type. Text is an array of `char`, and the end of the text is marked by a byte with value 0, written `'\0'` and called the NUL terminator. The string "Geeks" is therefore six bytes: G, e, e, k, s and 0. Functions that take a string receive only a `char *` to the first byte. They have no idea how large the underlying array is, so they trust the terminator to stop them.

This design is minimal and fast, and it shapes everything: the length of a string is not stored (you count to find it), copying needs room for one more byte than the visible length, and any code that forgets the terminator or the capacity runs off the end of the buffer. Learning strings in C is mostly learning to track three things at once: where the string starts, where it ends, and how much space exists after the start.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **NUL terminator**: the byte `'\0'` (value 0) that ends a string. It is not part of the length but it does occupy a byte.
**String length**: the number of characters before the terminator. `strlen("Geeks")` is 5, while the array needs at least 6 bytes.
**Character array**: `char s[] = "hi";` creates a writable array of 3 bytes (h, i, 0) initialized from the literal.

**String literal**: text in double quotes. It has static storage, has type `char[N+1]`, and must never be modified. Modifying one is undefined behavior and typically crashes because the data sits in read-only memory.
**Pointer to a string**: `const char *p = "hi";` stores the address of the first character of the literal. You cannot grow or change what it points at.
**Capacity versus length**: the array size is how much you may store, the length is how much you did store. Safe code compares them.
**`char` signedness**: plain `char` may be signed or unsigned depending on the platform, so passing it to `isalpha` and friends requires a cast to `unsigned char`.
**`<string.h>`**: the standard header for `strlen`, `strcpy`, `strncpy`, `strcat`, `strcmp`, `strchr`, `strstr`, `memcpy` and related functions.
**Scanset**: `%[...]` in `scanf` selects which characters to read, such as `%19[^\n]` for a whole line.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body:
Declaring `char s[] = "Geeks";` asks the compiler to size the array by counting the literal plus its terminator, so `sizeof s` is 6. The initializer is copied into `s`, which lives where the variable lives (the stack for a local). You can edit it freely: `s[0] = 'R'` is fine. Declaring `const char *p = "Geeks";` creates no array at all. It creates a pointer variable that holds the address of the literal's bytes in the read-only data section.

Every operation is a loop that stops at the terminator. Length counting reads bytes until it sees 0 and returns the count, so it costs O(n). Copying reads and writes bytes until it has copied the 0. Comparing walks two strings in step until the bytes differ or both end. The functions below show how little machinery that takes.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **Writable array**: `char s[] = "text";` a private copy you can modify, sized exactly to the literal unless you give a bigger size such as `char s[64] = "text";`.
**Pointer to literal**: `const char *s = "text";` shares one read-only copy, can be re-pointed, cannot be edited. Use `const` so the compiler catches writes.
**Heap string**: `char *s = malloc(n + 1);` or `strdup(t)` (POSIX, and standard in C23). You choose the size at run time and must `free` it.
**Array of strings**: `const char *names[] = {"ls", "cat", "grep"};` is an array of pointers to literals. `char grid[3][8]` is a rectangular block of three 8-byte strings instead.
**Counted string**: a struct with a `char *data` and a `size_t len`. Used by Pascal strings, many network protocols and most modern libraries, so embedded zero bytes and O(1) length work.
**Wide and multibyte strings**: `wchar_t` strings use `wcslen` and friends, and UTF-8 stored in plain `char` arrays uses 1 to 4 bytes per character, so `strlen` counts bytes, not characters.
**Bounded variants**: `strncpy`, `strncat`, `snprintf`, `strnlen`, `strlcpy` (BSD) trade the unbounded behavior of their cousins for explicit limits, each with its own quirks.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **strlen**: O(n), since the length is found by scanning. Calling it in a loop condition makes the loop O(n^2): `for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)`.

**strcpy, strcat, strcmp, strchr**: O(n) in the string length. `strcat` must first find the end of the destination, so building a long string with repeated `strcat` calls is O(n^2) in total. Keep a running end pointer instead.
**strstr**: O(n*m) worst case for the naive search. Good libc versions use two-way or similar algorithms to guarantee linear time.
**Memory**: `len + 1` bytes per string. A `char *` array holding k short strings spends 8 bytes per pointer on 64-bit plus the text.
**Literal sharing**: identical literals may be merged by the compiler, so a program with 1000 copies of "error" can still contain one copy.
**Comparison**: `==` on two `char *` compares addresses in O(1) and is almost never what you want. `strcmp` compares contents.
**Formatting**: `snprintf` returns the length the full output would have had, so you can detect truncation by comparing the result with the buffer size.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Missing room for the terminator**: `char s[5] = "Geeks";` fits the letters but has no terminator, so `printf("%s", s)` reads past the array. The array must be at least 6 bytes.
**Modifying a literal**: `char *p = "abc"; p[0] = 'x';` is undefined behavior and usually a segmentation fault. Declare `const char *p` or use an array.
**Comparing with `==`**: `if (name == "admin")` compares pointers and may be true or false depending on the compiler. Use `strcmp(name, "admin") == 0`.
**`strcpy` into too small a buffer**: nothing checks the destination size. It is the textbook stack buffer overflow. Check `strlen(src) < sizeof dst` first or use `snprintf`.

**`strncpy` is not a safe `strcpy`**: if the source is as long as the limit, it does not write a terminator. If shorter, it pads the rest with zeros, wasting time. Always set `dst[n-1] = '\0'` afterwards.
**`scanf("%s")` without a width**: reads any amount of text into your buffer. Write `%31s` for a 32-byte buffer, or use `fgets`.
**Forgetting the newline from `fgets`**: the buffer includes the trailing `'\n'`, which breaks later comparisons. Strip it with `strcspn`.
**`sizeof` versus `strlen`**: `sizeof s` is the array capacity including the terminator, `strlen(s)` is the current length. On a `char *` parameter, `sizeof` gives the pointer size.
**`strtok` modifies its input and keeps hidden state**: it overwrites delimiters with zeros, fails on literals and is not thread-safe. Prefer `strtok_r` or manual scanning.
**Treating `char` as always positive**: with bytes above 127 a plain `char` may be negative, which breaks table lookups and `isalpha` unless cast to `unsigned char`.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Command-line arguments**: `argv` is an array of `char *` strings, ended by a null pointer.
**File paths and environment**: `fopen`, `open`, `getenv` and `execve` all take NUL-terminated strings. A path with an embedded zero byte is silently cut short, a known source of injection bugs.
**Text protocols**: HTTP request lines, SMTP and many config formats are parsed in place by scanning for delimiters and replacing them with terminators.
**Logging and formatting**: `snprintf` into a fixed buffer is the standard way to build messages safely in firmware and kernels.
**Security**: classic exploits, such as the Morris worm via `gets` and format-string attacks via `printf(user_input)`, come from unchecked string handling.
**Kernel and embedded**: the Linux kernel avoids `strcpy` and `strncpy` in favour of `strscpy`, which always terminates and reports truncation.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **Q: What is a C string?** A char array ending with `'\0'`. The length is computed by scanning for it.

**Q: Difference between `char s[] = "hi"` and `char *s = "hi"`?** The first is a writable 3-byte array with a copy of the text. The second is a pointer to read-only literal data that must not be modified.
**Q: How much space does a string of length n need?** n + 1 bytes.
**Q: Why is `strncpy` considered dangerous?** It may leave the destination unterminated and pads with zeros when the source is short.
**Q: How would you reverse a string in place?** Two indices from both ends swapping until they meet, O(n) time and O(1) space.
**Q: How do you read a line safely?** `fgets` with the buffer size, then strip the newline. Never `gets`.
**Q: Why not `==` for strings?** It compares addresses. Use `strcmp`.
**Q: What does `sizeof("abc")` return?** 4, because the literal is a `char[4]` including the terminator.

subtopics.title: Declaring and initializing strings
subtopics.summary: Array, literal pointer and heap forms side by side.

sections.body: `char a[] = "Hi";` copies the text into a writable 3-byte array. `char b[10] = "Hi";` copies it into a bigger array and zero-fills the remaining 7 bytes. `char c[] = {'H', 'i', '\0'};` is the same as the first form spelled out. `const char *d = "Hi";` points at the literal. The only dangerous mistake is leaving out the terminator, as in `char e[] = {'H', 'i'};`, which is a valid char array but not a string.
sections.code:
char a[]   = "Hi";                // 3 bytes: H i \0
char b[10] = "Hi";                // 10 bytes: H i \0 \0 \0 \0 \0 \0 \0 \0
const char *d = "Hi";             // pointer to read-only data
printf("%zu %zu %zu\n", sizeof a, sizeof b, sizeof d);   // 3 10 8 on 64-bit

subtopics.title: Reading and writing strings
subtopics.summary: scanf, scansets, fgets, puts and printf, and what each does with whitespace and capacity.

sections.body: `printf("%s", s)` prints from the address until the terminator. `scanf("%s", buf)` stops at the first whitespace, so "Geeks For Geeks" yields only "Geeks". A scanset such as `%19[^\n]` reads up to 19 characters until a newline, spaces included. `fgets` reads a full line into a buffer with an explicit size and keeps the newline.
sections.code:
char word[16], line[32];
scanf("%15s", word);              // one token, at most 15 chars + terminator
scanf(" %31[^\n]", line);         // leading space skips pending whitespace
fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin);  // line with spaces, bounded by sizeof

subtopics.title: Standard string functions
subtopics.summary: The core of string.h with their exact behavior and risks.

bullets: `strlen(s)`: count of characters before the terminator, type `size_t`.
`strcpy(d, s)`: copies including the terminator, no bounds check.
`strncpy(d, s, n)`: copies at most n bytes, pads with zeros, may not terminate.
`strcat(d, s)` and `strncat(d, s, n)`: append `s` after the end of `d`. `strncat` always terminates and its limit counts only the appended characters.
`strcmp(a, b)` and `strncmp`: return negative, zero or positive according to the first differing byte, compared as unsigned char.
`strchr(s, c)` and `strrchr`: first and last occurrence of a character, or `NULL`.
`strstr(h, n)`: first occurrence of substring `n` in `h`, or `NULL`.
`memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`, `memcmp`: work on raw bytes with explicit counts, so they handle data with embedded zeros. Use `memmove` when ranges overlap.

subtopics.title: Strings and pointers
subtopics.summary: Walking a string by pointer, and why the array form and pointer form differ.

sections.body: A `char *` pointing at the first character is all a string function needs. Walking is a loop that advances until `*p == '\0'`. Subtracting two pointers into the same string gives a character count, which is how `strlen` and many parsers are written. The pointer form lets you re-point (`p = "other"`), the array form does not (`s = "other"` is a compile error), but only the array form owns bytes you may modify.

subtopics.title: String literals and read-only memory
subtopics.summary: Why modifying a literal crashes, and how const helps.

sections.body: A literal such as "Hello World" has static storage duration and is typically placed in a read-only section, so a store through a pointer to it triggers a segmentation fault. The C type of a literal is `char[N]`, not `const char[N]`, for historical reasons, so the compiler will not warn unless you enable `-Wwrite-strings` or declare the pointer `const`. Two equal literals may or may not share storage, so never depend on pointer equality.

subtopics.title: Arrays of strings
subtopics.summary: Pointer arrays versus 2D char arrays, and iterating argv.

sections.body: `const char *names[3]` stores three pointers (24 bytes on 64-bit) to literals of any length. `char names[3][8]` stores 24 bytes of text with every row 8 bytes, wasting space for short names but keeping the text writable and contiguous. `argv` is the pointer form, and `argv[argc]` is `NULL`.

subtopics.title: Converting between strings and numbers
subtopics.summary: strtol and snprintf instead of atoi and sprintf.

sections.body: `atoi` returns 0 for garbage and cannot report overflow. `strtol(s, &end, 10)` parses a number, sets `end` to the first unparsed character and sets `errno` to `ERANGE` on overflow. Check `end != s` and `*end == '\0'` to be sure the whole string was a number. For the reverse direction use `snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%d", n)`, never `sprintf`, which has no limit.

subtopics.title: Safe string handling and buffer overflow
subtopics.summary: The habits that prevent the classic security bugs.

bullets: Know the capacity of every buffer and pass it along with the pointer.
Prefer `snprintf` and `fgets`. Treat `gets`, `strcpy`, `strcat` and `sprintf` with unchecked input as bugs.
Always leave room for the terminator and verify truncation by checking the return value of `snprintf`.
Never pass user input as the format string: write `printf("%s", s)`, not `printf(s)`.
Build with `-Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address` during testing to catch overflows.

subtopics.title: Implementing string utilities
subtopics.summary: Reverse and palindrome check, the two most common interview programs.

sections.body: Both use two indices that start at the ends and move toward each other, so they run in O(n) time and O(1) space. For the palindrome check, compare characters and stop at the first mismatch. For case-insensitive or punctuation-skipping versions, advance each index past characters you ignore and compare with `tolower((unsigned char)c)`.

takeaways: A C string is a char array ending in `'\0'`; a string of length n needs n + 1 bytes.
`strlen` scans for the terminator, so it is O(n) and should not sit in a loop condition.
`char s[] = "x"` is a writable copy; `const char *p = "x"` points at read-only data and must never be modified.
Never compare strings with `==`; use `strcmp`, which returns zero when they match.
`strcpy`, `strcat`, `sprintf`, `gets` and unbounded `scanf("%s")` do not check capacity; prefer `snprintf` and `fgets`.
`strncpy` may leave the destination unterminated, so terminate manually.
`fgets` keeps the newline; strip it with `strcspn(line, "\n")`.
In UTF-8 text `strlen` returns bytes, not characters.
